extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and screenwriters seeking a systematic story-structure method
extracted.subtask_description: Apply John Truby's Anatomy of Story 22-step framework to design character-driven plots where inner change (self-revelation) and moral argument shape the story. Useful for novelists and screenwriters building integrated character-and-plot structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing premise
rubrics_metrics.description: "All stories have a premise, but only good stories have a designing premise." Premise = your story in one line; designing premise = the premise that creates the story; the seed from which everything grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The designing premise should organize every part of the story—theme, character, plot—and act as the generative idea that determines structure and moral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Self-revelation, need, and desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Protagonist's inner psychology: their self-revelation, need, and desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish what the protagonist must discover about themselves and what they consciously want versus what they truly need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Ghost and story world
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory wound (the 'ghost') and the world that shaped the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the formative wound that drives choices and the social/physical world that conditioned the character's behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 3 — Weakness and need
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and psychological flaws and what the protagonist must learn (their need).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between surface desire (goal) and deeper moral/psychological need; structure scenes to expose and test these weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 4 — Inciting event
rubrics_metrics.description: An event that disrupts the protagonist's world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the inciting event meaningful to the protagonist's ghost/need so it propels inner and outer change rather than being merely plot-driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5 — Desire
rubrics_metrics.description: What the protagonist consciously wants (the goal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the protagonist's conscious desire clear and specific so it can be contrasted with deeper needs and changed through revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 6 — Ally or allies
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who help the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allies should play active roles that test and reveal aspects of the protagonist; they are part of the character web and can provoke growth or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 7 — Opponent and/or mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: The antagonist or the puzzle standing in opposition to the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opponent should embody the counter-argument to the protagonist's moral stance or create difficult obstacles that force choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 8 — Fake-ally opponent
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparent friend who is actually a foe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fake-allies to create betrayal and complexity in relationships; they reveal blind spots in the protagonist's judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 9 — First revelation and decision: changed desire and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist learns something and adjusts their desire and motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This first revelation should change the course of action and deepen stakes, showing the plot is driven by evolving inner knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 10 — Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's strategy to achieve their goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plans should be logical responses to revelations and obstacles, and their execution should expose character flaws and provoke conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 11 — Opponent's plan and main counterattack
rubrics_metrics.description: The antagonist's strategy and the primary counter-move against the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the opponent as an active force with a coherent plan that directly challenges the protagonist's plan and moral stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 12 — Drive
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist takes decisive action against the opponent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions should escalate conflict and reveal whether the protagonist's motives and plans are effective or flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 13 — Attack by ally
rubrics_metrics.description: Allies challenge the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allies should not be passive; their interventions can complicate the protagonist's journey and expose moral tensions within the character web.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 14 — Apparent defeat
rubrics_metrics.description: A point where it looks like all is lost for the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use apparent defeat to force deeper choices and set up the re-commitment that follows; it should feel earned by prior actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 15 — Second revelation and decision: obsessive drive, changed desire and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: A further revelation that drives obsessive action and again changes desire/motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deepening revelation should shift the protagonist toward either destructive obsession or clarified purpose, preparing for the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 16 — Audience revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Information revealed to readers/viewers that reframes events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use revelations strategically to align audience understanding with dramatic irony or to heighten stakes before the final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 17 — Third revelation and decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Another key discovery by the protagonist followed by a pivotal decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This revelation should make the final moral choice unavoidable and crystallize the protagonist's inner truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 18 — Gate, gauntlet, visit to death
rubrics_metrics.description: A trial or series of trials that the protagonist must face (a 'visit to death').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the trial to test both outer skills and inner transformation; it should feel like a near-death test of the protagonist's new values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 19 — Battle
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax—the decisive confrontation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The battle should resolve the central conflict in a way that is consistent with both the outer plot and the protagonist's inner change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 20 — Self-revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist realizes the truth about themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-revelation functions as the emotional/psychological climax and must be earned by the preceding story of wounds, choices, and revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 21 — Moral decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on self-revelation, the protagonist makes a moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral decision should answer the story's moral argument and demonstrate whether the protagonist accepts or rejects the new truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 22 — New equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: The new state of being after the story's resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how the protagonist and the story world have changed; the new equilibrium should reflect consequences of the moral decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is an argument about the right way to live; the protagonist's position is opposed by the antagonist's counter-argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the opposing moral positions and structure scenes so character choices illustrate and test those values; the climax should resolve the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-revelation as climax
rubrics_metrics.description: The inner change (self-revelation) functions as the climactic point of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the emotional/psychological discovery coincide with or drive the outer climax—inner revelation should determine the moral decision and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character web
rubrics_metrics.description: All major characters form an interlocking web of flaws and needs that reflect and test the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design relationships so each major character's weakness or need contrasts with or pressures the protagonist, creating thematic resonance across scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-as-organism
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part of the story is connected to every other part; the story behaves like an integrated organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid isolated scenes or characters; ensure that plot events, character choices, and thematic premises all derive from and support the designing premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Tests (checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short checklist for evaluating whether a story meets Truby's standards: Is there a designing premise? Does the protagonist have a clear ghost, weakness, need, desire? Does the antagonist embody the opposing moral argument? Does the climax produce self-revelation? Does self-revelation drive the moral decision? Are allies and opponents organized into a web of flaws?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a diagnostic after drafting to identify missing design elements or weak connections between character, plot, and moral argument.
